doc.title: Josiah Gluck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 13, 2022

title: Guest bands, Brandi Carlile and in-ear monitors
summary: Guest acts mostly bring touring bands; Gluck praises Brandi Carlile's unplugged set and explains how in-ears reduce leakage in SNL's fragile mixes.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Are you aware or not if the band that the singers bring are usually their touring people? Or are they sort of picked for the show?

It’s almost always touring. If someone has let’s say a bunch of horn players or they need a dozen strings then that will usually be a pick-up ensemble from the City. And you know, and in fact the music contractor we use, Sandy, who was the one playing violin in that thing, in that one story, I’ll see her often at the show with that kind of — you know a contractor bringing people in.
Just a personal aside I was happy to see a Hamilton alum from our college playing bass with Dua Lipa on Saturday Night Live. That was really cool. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Yeah she’s fun. She can sing, that’s a fun band. This past season probably the highlight for me was working with Brandi Carlisle. She was just sublime. You know great voice, great songs, great players. And it was just playing. It was like no click-track, no tracks or whatnot. And I don’t mean that in a dismissive way because you know playing back pre- recorded tracks or whatever sonic signature that has been created with loops and beats and editing and so forth you know from the get-go that is not something that is going to be necessarily replicated by people playing it. It’s a sound created in the studio and so if you want to have the performance to be as close as possible or somewhat similar to what you do on record, then you have to bring that along. And everyone plays in lock-step to it.
Do people use in-ear monitors on the show?

Yes. A great deal. And that’s been a huge help as far as cleaning up sound and making things tighter. You know I try to describe it to civilians as if you have a singer who’s kind of singing away from the mic and they’re not singing very loudly and they have a drummer behind them bashing away, it’s going to get into that mic. And as I say imagine you were to take a perfectly still like tub of water and take flower petals and arrange the most beautiful mosaic design just floating on the surface and everything’s working and all locked together. And then you pull the plug out the middle and everything just swirls and goes in and everything gets distorted because it all crashes into that one thing. And that to me is what happens when you have a lot of leakage that become an issue and half the battle with SNL is it’s like a sonic house of cards. How to we get all these pieces to fit. And it can be done with all sorts of tricks of compression and EQ and side chaining and other things that studio people might feel like [gasps] you can’t do that. You can’t put that much on. It’s like well how does it sound? Oh it actually sounds pretty good. Well then what does it matter? But it’s a completely different discipline than being in the studio.
